regulatory_subsections.old_united_states_value:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken action against companies marketing BPC-157 as a dietary supplement, stating it does not meet the definition of a legal supplement ingredient. As of 16 October 2026, BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23), and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published. FDA has also found some clinics compounding it. See "U.S. regulatory status — compounding review" below for the July 2026 advisory committee meeting and the October 2026 interim policy submitted for OIRA review.

Products sold as "research chemicals" are not FDA-regulated drugs. Many websites sell BPC-157 with disclaimers that it is not for human use. This grey market means quality control is questionable: products might not contain the stated amount or could have impurities.

old_compounding_subsection.title: U.S. regulatory status — compounding review (as of 16 October 2026)

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published as of 16 October 2026. In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and compounding: an advisory committee vote in July and an interim policy sent for White House review in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or makes it lawful to compound.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) met on 23–24 July 2026. On 23 July it considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the list of bulk drug substances that may be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the "503A Bulks List"). FDA evaluated both forms for ulcerative colitis. FDA's published voting questions were: "Should BPC-157 (free base) be placed on the list?" and "Should BPC-157 acetate be placed on the list?" In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither BPC-157 (free base) nor BPC-157 acetate be included on the 503A Bulks List. FDA states that advisory committee recommendations are non-binding. Reuters reported on 15 October 2026 that the advisers had recommended FDA loosen restrictions on six of the seven peptides reviewed in July, including BPC-157. As of 16 October 2026, FDA has not posted official minutes or vote tallies on the meeting page, so this entry gives no vote counts. The 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23) has not been amended to include BPC-157.

Interim access policy under OIRA review (received 14 October 2026). OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) lists a pending Executive Order 12866 review with these details. Title: "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides". Agency/Subagency: HHS / FDA. RIN: 0910-ZD94. Stage: Notice. Received Date: 10/14/2026. Legal Deadline: None. Economically Significant: No (OIRA listing as indexed; live page unavailable 16 Oct 2026). The listing does not name any peptides and does not include the policy text. As of 16 October 2026, no matching Federal Register document and no FDA press announcement were found. Reuters, citing an Associated Press report based on two unnamed people, reported that the policy would allow some popular peptides, including BPC-157, to be compounded. That is a press report and has not been confirmed in any published text.
Not an approval: neither the PCAC vote nor the OIRA submission is FDA approval of BPC-157 for any use.
No published text: the policy text has not been released, and no Federal Register notice has been located.
No effective or start date: none has been announced.
Scope unknown: the OIRA listing does not say which peptides would be covered.
Review is not a final policy: an OIRA review is a step before publication. The policy may be changed, withdrawn, or published in a different form.

Other status lines are unchanged: on FDA's "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" page (content current as of 22 April 2026), BPC-157 is listed as nominated but withdrawn. BPC-157 remains on WADA's S0 (non-approved substances) list.

Because BPC-157 has not been extensively studied in people, there could be side effects that haven't been observed in small samples. Minor side effects like headaches, dizziness, or injection site reactions might not show up in tiny studies but could in larger populations.

The "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" (RIN 0910-ZD94) has been under OIRA review since 14 October 2026. Its text has not been published, it has no effective date, and the peptides it covers are not known. PeptideMap does not predict outcomes.
